extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; economists; policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of 18th-century principles for measuring the value (price) of commodities and labour, including distinctions between real and nominal price, the role of labour, money, and commodity standards, and practical implications for rents and coinage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value in use vs value in exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'value' has two different meanings: sometimes it expresses the utility of some particular object ('value in use'), and sometimes the power of purchasing other goods which the possession of that object conveys ('value in exchange').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: water has great value in use but scarce any value in exchange; a diamond has little value in use but can be exchanged for a great quantity of other goods. Recognize and distinguish these two senses when discussing or measuring value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour as the real measure of exchangeable value
rubrics_metrics.description: Labour is the real measure of the exchangeable value of all commodities: the value of any commodity to a person who means to exchange it equals the quantity of labour which it enables him to purchase or command. 'Labour was the first price, the original purchase money that was paid for all things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'real price' as the toil and trouble of acquiring or what a commodity can save in toil; treat money or other goods as merely saving labour. Use labour (to the extent measurable) as the ultimate standard when comparing real values across times and places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real price (toil and trouble) versus nominal price (money)
rubrics_metrics.description: The real price of everything is the toil and trouble of acquiring it; the nominal price is the quantity of money. Labour and commodities have real and nominal prices: the labourer's welfare is determined by the real, not the nominal, price of his labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing welfare or long-term obligations, prioritize real prices (what goods or labour a sum commands) rather than nominal sums of money, because money's purchasing power can vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of accurately measuring labour across different employments
rubrics_metrics.description: Equal hours of different sorts of work do not always represent equal labour: differences of hardship, skill, and ingenuity mean the same time may involve very different labour. It is not easy to find any accurate measure either of hardship or ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, exchanges adjust these differences through market bargaining ('higgling and bargaining'), producing rough equality sufficient for ordinary commerce rather than precise equivalence. Be cautious about equating hours across trades without allowance for intensity and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: People estimate value more naturally by commodity or money than by labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Because commodities are more tangible and money is the common instrument of commerce, people more naturally estimate exchangeable value by quantities of other commodities or by money than by quantities of labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical valuation and price communication typically use money (or familiar commodities) rather than labour measures—for example, saying beef is 'threepence a-pound' rather than 'worth X hours of labour.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability of money (gold and silver) makes it only a nominal standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Gold and silver, like other commodities, vary in value depending on factors such as the fertility or barrenness of mines. A commodity which itself continually varies in its own value can never be an accurate measure of the value of other commodities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that money is an exact measure of value only 'at the same time and place.' For comparisons across time or place, adjustments for changes in the value of the metal (or money supply) are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of comparative standard depends on timeframe (labour, corn, silver)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equal quantities of labour are always of equal value to the labourer and are the ultimate standard; equal quantities of corn are a better measure than silver from century to century, while silver is a better measure than corn from year to year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing real values across long historical spans, prefer commodity standards that track subsistence (corn). For shorter-term comparisons, metal money (silver) may approximate labour-commanding power more closely. Use labour as the ultimate reference when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of rent reservation affects preservation of value
rubrics_metrics.description: Rents reserved in money are liable to variations arising from changes in the metal content of coins and from changes in the value of the metal; rents reserved in corn have preserved their value much better than money rents historically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For perpetual or very long-term obligations intended to keep constant real value, prefer in-kind reservations (e.g., corn) or payments indexed to a commodity rather than a fixed nominal monetary sum. Historical examples: college rents reserved in corn retained value better than money rents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal tender, chosen standard metal, and regulated proportions influence perceived standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations generally coin several metals for money but consider one metal as the measure of value (the one first used). When governments legally fix proportions between metals (e.g., guinea to shillings), the custom of accounting in one metal makes that metal appear the standard and affects how values are perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in the regulated proportion (recoinage, legal-tender rules) can shift which metal seems to 'measure' value and alter the relative quantities required to discharge debts. Account-keeping customs matter in which metal is treated as standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mint price, market price, export rules, and coin reformation affect bullion and coin values
rubrics_metrics.description: The mint gives a specified quantity of coin for a weight of bullion (mint price). Market price of bullion can be above or below mint price; export permissions/prohibitions and coin reformation (changing weight/fineness) influence these relationships and thus the market value of bullion versus coin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from England: mint prices for gold and silver are given; reformation of the gold coin raised the market value of silver coin in proportion to gold. Policies on exporting bullion or coin can change demand and thus market prices (the text critiques simple explanations such as Locke's).

rubrics_metrics.name: Merchants judge profit and make transactions by money price differences regardless of differing real values across places
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where an ounce of silver commands different quantities of labour at different places (e.g., Canton vs London), a merchant's calculations and prudence rest on nominal money prices: if he can buy for half an ounce and sell for an ounce, he gains 100% as measured by money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For trade decisions, focus on the nominal price differences convertible into the merchant's accounting currency rather than differing local real-command-of-labour values; practical commerce operates on money-price arbitrage.
